newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: After 80 days, protesters still target Milosevic.
newsitem.headline: After 80 days, protesters still target Milosevic.

text.p: Serbian opposition supporters danced, sang, whistled and banged pots and pans on the 80th day of colourful protests and their leaders warned they will not let President Slobodan Milosevic off the hook.

With just two days to go before parliament is due to reinstate opposition victories in local elections, the Zajedno (Together) coalition said on Friday it would challenge Milosevic in general elections later this year.
The official Yugoslav news agency Tanjug said the bill, approved by Milosevic's Socialist government on Wednesday, reached parliament on Friday ahead of Tuesday's meeting.
Milosevic suddenly announced three days ago he was asking parliament to approve a new law recognising the opposition's victories, a central plank of their campaign for democratic and economic reform.

"Our reality is catastrophic. Our economy is virtually non-existent and all state coffers virtually empty. The state is on the brink of poverty," Zajedno leader Vuk Draskovic told 50,000 supporters in Belgrade's central square on Friday.
"Our salvation lies in a powerful Serbia accepted by the world -- but the world will only accept a democratic Serbia.
"All economic programmes are completely worthless unless the political system is changed. Our main objective is thus democracy," he said.

Zoran Djindjic, who leads Zajedno together with Draskovic and Vesna Pesic, accused the authorities of corruption and said it was "now trying to complete the wholesale rape of Serbia" by its privatisation concept.
He accused the authorities of deliberately pauperising state firms and then selling them to friends "for peanuts".
"Those factories were funded by all of us, not by the state, which now aims to sell them off as if it owned them."
Djindjic, billed as the next mayor of Belgrade, urges a privatisation model applied in the Czech republic or Slovenia where workers were given stakes in new firms.
The crowd cheered as Rade Radovanovic, an opposition union leader, gave the three Zajedno leaders a 52-kg piece of the Berlin Wall donated by the Association of Victims of Undemocratic Regimes.
He said a much bigger chunk of the wall -- demolished after the collapse of communism in East Germany in 1989 -- would be set up in Belgrade "after the victory of democracy in Serbia".
Draskovic awarded the stone souvenir to the students who had organised parallel demonstrations for the past 80 days.
About 15,000 students marched through Belgrade earlier in the day, maintaining pressure on Milosevic to keep his promise, but Zajedno was sceptical he would deliver.
"We will wait for the decision of parliament but until then the demonstrations will continue for sure," Zajedno spokesman Slobodan Vuksanovic told a news conference on Friday.
International law expert Vojin Dimitrijevic warned Milosevic could have another trick up his sleeve.

"After a couple of days, when people disperse from the streets, it would be quite possible to summon the obedient supreme constitutional court of Yugoslavia which would annul this law -- and rightly so," he warned.
The ultra-nationalist Serbian Radical Party led by Vojislav Seselj, once a close ally of Milosevic, has already said it would appeal to the constitutional court against the bill.
As dusk fell on the capital, people came to windows or onto their balconies to create their usual din with pots and pans.
Others marched or blocked streets. Actors porotested in front of Belgrade's Drama Theatre against police violence.

On Sunday, dreaded police the opposition call Milosevic's "Praetorian Guards" swooped on peaceful protesters in the worst violence since tanks were used in 1991 to quell dissent. The move backfired in an outcry by the West when thousands showed up at demonstrations again the next day.
